name: Negative Latitude
description: The debut feature of collective director-duo Seren Okafor-Brandt and Mikael Tuulikki, this experimental neural-feed offers no protagonist and no linear narrative — instead the viewer inhabits a sequence of forty-seven sensory states experienced by people who have undergone involuntary memory erasure as corporate debt settlement. The feed induces controlled synesthesia, translating grief into color temperatures and loss of identity into spatial disorientation that lingers for hours after disconnection. It was never formally distributed; copies were loaded directly onto willing recipients' BCIs at a single underground event in 2186 and propagated peer-to-peer from there.
cultural_impact: Considered the founding artifact of the 'erasure cinema' movement and referenced in nearly every subsequent discussion of neuroethics in immersive media.
story_hooks: One of the forty-seven memory sequences in the film appears to be a real, non-consenting person's actual erased memory — and that person is still alive.
A corporate intelligence division is quietly collecting everyone who has a copy of the feed, cataloguing them as potential subversives.
Seren Okafor-Brandt claims the film contains a hidden forty-eighth state accessible only when two people experience it simultaneously via linked BCIs — no one has verified this.
